speaking-mock-4.title: US economic strength
speaking-mock-4.text: One way to understand a country's economic strength is by looking at the size of economy. In terms of overall economic size, the United States produces more than the total amount of several major economies, including China, Japan, the UK, and Germany. This comparison highlights the significant role the United States plays in the global economy. Another important indicator is the industrial output. US output is approximately $2.8 trillion, making it one of the largest manufacturing sectors in the world. Interestingly, this figure equals to the sum of China and Japan, showing the remarkable scale of American industrial production. Although many countries continue to expand their economies, the United States remains one of the world's leading economic powers
facts: The lecture uses total economic size and industrial output as indicators of economic strength.
The speaker compares the US economy with China, Japan, the UK and Germany.
US industrial output is stated to be approximately $2.8 trillion and compared with the combined output of China and Japan.
The overall argument presents the US as a leading global economic power.
speaking-mock-4.sample: The lecture explains that economic strength can be assessed through total economic size and industrial output. The speaker compares the United States with several major economies and cites industrial production of approximately 2.8 trillion dollars. This manufacturing output is described as comparable to the combined output of China and Japan. The lecture concludes that the United States remains one of the world's leading economic powers.

speaking-mock-4.instruction: Listen to the lecture, then retell its main ideas and relevant supporting details in your own words.
speaking-mock-4.title: Earth v.s. Mars
speaking-mock-4.text: Scientists often compare the conditions on the Earth and Mars to evaluate the habitability of Mars. There are some similarities between Earth and Mars. Both planets have polar caps, atmospheres, and evidence of a water-related climate. The lecture also describes different forms of water on Earth and Mars. On Earth, it exists as oceans, while on Mars, water is present in the form of ice. Despite these similarities, however, there are still lots of differences between the two worlds. Even the most inhabitable areas on the earth are way different from those on Mars. In preparing for the Phoenix Mission, scientists have conducted Antarctica trial runs. During these tests, researchers dug trenches, collected samples, and examined the ice-soil boundary. These Antarctic experiments serve as practical simulations, helping scientists get ready for investigations on Mars.
facts: Earth and Mars are compared to assess the habitability of Mars.
Both planets have polar caps, atmospheres and evidence of water-related conditions.
Earth's oceans are contrasted with ice on Mars, alongside substantial planetary differences.
Antarctic trials for the Phoenix Mission involved trenches, samples and the ice-soil boundary to prepare for Martian investigations.
speaking-mock-4.sample: The lecture compares Earth and Mars in relation to the habitability of Mars. Both planets have polar caps, atmospheres and water-related conditions, although Earth's oceans differ from the ice found on Mars. The speaker also describes Antarctic trials undertaken for the Phoenix Mission. Researchers dug trenches, collected samples and examined the ice-soil boundary, using these activities as simulations to prepare for investigations on Mars.

speaking-mock-4.name: Summarise Group Discussion
speaking-mock-4.instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
speaking-mock-4.title: Making the university more eco-friendly
speaking-mock-4.narration: Three students are discussing how to make their university more eco-friendly.
turns: Speaker 1

Hey fellas, I think there is still room for improvement when it comes to making our campus more eco-friendly. The staff should install recycling stations on key spots around the university, making it convenient for us to recycle plastic bottles, which can reduce landfill waste.
Speaker 2

Actually, we should reduce waste from the source, namely, reduce the amount of waste produced by us instead of having more bins. Just the campus cafe alone uses hundreds of paper cups every day. People should use fewer single-use coffee cups at the cafe and bring their own reusable cups.
Speaker 3

You are right. It is good for the cafeteria to use recycled paper, but they give out too many napkins at one time. Also, some packaging is too excessive, such as five layers of packaging for an apple.
Speaker 1
Yes, and students can also play a role here. We should take only what we actually need and avoid wasting food, paper, and other resources, by which we would also save money in the long run.
Speaker 3

If students bring their own bottles and cups, the university could reduce the amount of waste while students could develop more environmentally friendly habits. Another thing is more sustainable transportation. The university should build better bike paths, and provide more bike parking spaces, in order to encourage students to ride bikes with dual benefits, which is eco-friendly and great for their physical health.
Speaker 2
For students rushing between lectures, bicycles can cut their travel time. But there would be limited impact because few students own bikes. The university should establish a shared bicycle station.
Speaker 3
That sounds practical because students would not need to buy or maintain their own bicycles. They could simply rent a bike when they need one and return it after class.
Speaker 1

The university should also encourage carpooling, like having cheap parking to reward carpooling students or even free parking. It can also reduce the number of cars on campus and lower traffic congestion, especially during busy hours in the morning and afternoon.
Speaker 2

Yes, carpooling allows students to get together. Anyway, better public transport should also be considered, like buses or trains. If public transport is more convenient and reliable, students may be less dependent on private cars. This could make a bigger difference in the long term.
Speaker 1

We are a part of this green community, and should join in the eco-friendly movement. There are a lot of things to do, but we should start from small ones by ourselves, like bringing our own cups to the cafeteria, and carpooling.
facts: The group discusses reducing university waste and making transport more sustainable.
Speaker 1 proposes convenient recycling stations, using only needed resources and parking incentives for carpooling.
Speaker 2 prioritises preventing waste at its source by replacing disposable coffee cups with reusable cups.
Speaker 3 criticises excessive napkins and packaging and supports reusable bottles and cups.
Speaker 3 proposes better bike paths and parking; Speaker 2 adds shared bicycles because few students own bikes, and Speaker 3 supports renting them.
Speaker 2 also advocates reliable public transport to reduce car dependence.
They support both university improvements and small personal actions such as reusable cups and carpooling.
speaking-mock-4.sample: The students discuss making their university greener through waste reduction and sustainable transport. The first speaker proposes recycling stations, avoiding unnecessary resource use and encouraging carpooling with cheaper parking. The second argues that preventing waste is more useful than adding bins and recommends reusable cups. The third agrees and criticises excessive packaging and napkins, then suggests better cycling facilities. The second adds a bike-sharing scheme because few students own bicycles and calls for more reliable public transport. The third supports shared bikes as a convenient alternative to ownership. Overall, they favour practical campus improvements alongside personal habits such as reusing cups and sharing journeys.

speaking-mock-4.name: Summarise Group Discussion
speaking-mock-4.instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
speaking-mock-4.title: Tackling a college essay
speaking-mock-4.narration: Three students are discussing how to tackle the challenge of writing a college essay.
turns: Speaker 1

Guys, I'm really struggling with this essay. It's so much more difficult than high school, and I have no idea where to start. It's just overwhelming. I keep rereading the prompt, but I'm still not sure if I'm interpreting it correctly.
Speaker 2

Hey, don't worry too much about it. The first thing you should do is to make sure you understand the question. Trying to write without a clear idea of what you're supposed to be discussing will just make things harder. Maybe try breaking the prompt down into smaller parts or even talk to your professor after class to clarify what they're looking for.
Speaker 3

Yeah. You don't need to start by writing the summary or introduction. Just start with the main content first. Get all your ideas down, and then you can organize them into a logical order later. I always do a brain dump first just writing everything I know or think about the topic without worrying about structure.
Speaker 2

That's true. Once you have your main points, you can write a draft and then go back and revise. You might find it easier to write the summary once you've done that. And don't forget, we're here to help, too. We can proofread your draft and give you some feedback. If you want, we could even set up a study session this weekend to go over your outline together.
Speaker 1
That sounds like a good plan. I feel much better about this now. I think I'll try the brain dump method tonight and then maybe share my rough points with you tomorrow.
Speaker 3
The writing center on campus is also a great resource. They can help you brainstorm ideas and even review your essay before you submit it.
Speaker 2

Exactly, don't hesitate to use the resources available to you. And take breaks too when you find yourself stuck. Sometimes stepping away for a bit can help clear your mind and give you a fresh perspective. I always set a timer like 45 minutes of writing, then a 10-minute break. It keeps me from burning out.
Speaker 1

Yeah, you guys make a lot of sense. I'll start by understanding the question and then move on from there. And I'll definitely use the writing center's help, too. Thank you so much! I was so stressed earlier, but now I actually have a clear starting point.
Speaker 3

You're welcome! Just remember to take it one step at a time. Writing an essay doesn't have to be a huge, insurmountable task. You're capable of breaking it down and conquering it, piece by piece. And honestly, your first draft doesn't have to be perfect just getting something on paper is already progress.
Speaker 2
Exactly, remember we're only a call away. We all struggle at times, but that's how we learn and grow. You've got this!
facts: The discussion concerns helping a student who feels overwhelmed by a college essay and is unsure about the prompt.
Speaker 2 recommends understanding the question, breaking it into parts or asking the professor for clarification.
Speaker 3 recommends brainstorming or a brain dump before organising the main content; the introduction or summary can wait.
Speaker 2 offers peer proofreading, feedback and a study session, and recommends regular breaks to avoid burnout.
Speaker 3 recommends the campus writing center and reassures the student that an imperfect first draft is progress.
Speaker 1 feels reassured and plans to clarify the question, brainstorm, share ideas and use the writing center.
speaking-mock-4.sample: The students discuss how to approach a difficult college essay. The first speaker feels overwhelmed and is unsure how to interpret the prompt. The second recommends breaking down the question or asking the professor for clarification, then drafting and revising with peer feedback. The third suggests getting ideas down before worrying about structure and using the campus writing center. The second also recommends regular breaks to avoid burnout, while the third stresses that an imperfect first draft is still progress. The first speaker accepts this advice and plans to brainstorm, share rough points and seek support. Overall, the discussion moves from anxiety to a manageable writing plan.

speaking-mock-4.title: A friend talking during a lecture
speaking-mock-4.text: Your friend is sitting next to you and keeps talking, but you want to focus on the lecture and take notes. What would you say to him?
facts: Speak directly and politely to the friend.
Explain the need to concentrate on the lecture and take notes.
Ask to continue the conversation later.
speaking-mock-4.sample: Hey, could we talk after the lecture? I need to concentrate and take notes so I do not miss anything. Let us catch up when the class finishes. Thanks for understanding.

speaking-mock-5.name: Retell Lecture
speaking-mock-5.instruction: Listen to the lecture, then retell its main ideas and relevant supporting details in your own words.
speaking-mock-5.title: Neurons and the coding of intensity
speaking-mock-5.text: One interesting thing about neurons is a neuron is like a gun. It either fires or it doesn't. It's all or nothing. If you squeeze the trigger of a gun really hard and really fast, it doesn't fire any faster or harder than if you just squeezed it gently. Now, this seems to be strange. Why? How could neurons be all or nothing when sensation is very graded? If somebody next to you pushed on your hand - the degree of pushing - you'd be able to notice it. It's not either pushing or not pushing. You can - Degrees of pushing, degrees of heat, degrees of brightness. And the answer is, although neurons are all or nothing, there are ways to code intensity. So, one simple way to code intensity is the number of neurons firing, the more neurons the more intense. Another way to increase intensity is the frequency of firing. So, I'll just use those two. The first one is the number of neurons firing. The second one is the frequency of firing in that something is more intense if it's "bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang" then "bang, bang, bang" and these are two ways through which neurons encode intensity.
facts: Individual neurons follow an all-or-nothing firing principle, illustrated by a gun trigger.
Sensations such as pressure, heat and brightness have different degrees of intensity.
Intensity can be encoded by the number of neurons firing.
A higher frequency of neuronal firing is another way to encode greater intensity.
speaking-mock-5.sample: The lecture explains how neurons encode the intensity of sensations. Although an individual neuron either fires or does not fire, people can distinguish different degrees of pressure, heat and brightness. The speaker identifies two ways to represent this variation: increasing the number of neurons that fire and increasing their firing frequency. Thus graded sensations can be encoded through the activity of all-or-nothing neurons.

speaking-mock-5.title: Science and Scientist
speaking-mock-5.text:
Female: Which one are you going to write more in your book, science or scientists?
Male: I do want very much to write something about science, actually. So I prefer to scientists.
Female: All right. What's interesting in scientists then?
Male: Science is just like complex furniture, which is all about evidence. But scientists can tell stories, do researches and propose questions to find what is true. They are like a focal point. They are always in interesting situations.
Female: Whether science or scientists your book mainly about, it seems to be rather hard for general readers to understand, doesn't it?
Male: I don't think so, really. In fact the book I write is a science fiction, which is related with science but is not strictly scientific. So you don't have to have a PhD degree in physics or other disciplines to understand a science fiction. And loving science is very different from being a scientist, which means fiction writing is not the same as writing scientific journals. When scientists fail, they will question the situation about why they have failed. But as a fiction writer, I don't have to. In my book, you can always see stories about 'happy family'.
facts: The discussion concerns whether a book focuses on science or scientists.
The writer finds scientists interesting because they ask questions, investigate and tell stories.
The book is science fiction rather than a strictly scientific journal.
The writer says general readers need no specialist PhD to understand the book and distinguishes fiction writing from scientific research.
speaking-mock-5.sample: The speakers discuss a writer's interest in science and scientists. He finds scientists appealing because they investigate questions and provide interesting stories. He explains that his book is science fiction rather than a strictly scientific work, so readers do not need a specialist degree to understand it. The discussion also distinguishes enjoying science and writing fiction from working as a scientist or publishing scientific journals.

speaking-mock-5.name: Summarise Group Discussion
speaking-mock-5.instruction: Listen to three speakers. Summarise the topic, each person’s contribution, and how their views relate to one another.
speaking-mock-5.title: Campus part-time jobs
speaking-mock-5.narration: Three students are debating the pros and cons of campus part-time jobs, gathered at a corner table in the student lounge, the air filled with the faint smell of coffee and the rustle of textbook pages.
turns: Speaker 1

I think working part-time on campus is a total waste of energy. Last month I took a job at the library desk, and between shelving books and scanning IDs, I barely had any mental capacity left for my coursework. I ended up dozing off during my morning lectures twice last week.
Speaker 2

Actually, I find my part-time job at the academic office really helpful. It forces me to manage my time better. I used to procrastinate all afternoon, but now I block out my shifts and study hours in advance. Plus, I'm earning my own spending money it feels good not to have to ask my parents for every little thing.
Speaker 3

But the workload is no joke. I tried working at the campus café last semester and it drained me completely. Some days I'd finish my shift at 8 pm, and then still have to write a lab report due at midnight. I got so stressed I had to quit after a month. It's not just about time it's the mental toll.
Speaker 1

Exactly! And let's be honest most of these jobs don't even relate to our future careers. I'd rather join a student club or work on a project that actually builds my resume. Stuffing envelopes or swiping cards isn't going to help me get into grad school.
Speaker 2

I see what you mean, but you're overlooking the soft skills. I've learned to talk to supervisors, handle complaints, and show up on time that's real-world experience. And it's not always about the job itself; it's about showing you can balance responsibilities.
Speaker 3

I guess, but I still think it depends on your schedule. If you're taking 18 credits like I am this semester, adding a job is just unrealistic. The stress isn't sustainable. Maybe if the university limited work hours to under 10 per week... but even then, I'd rather use that time to review or sleep.
Speaker 1

Same. I'd prefer a work-study program that's more flexible and aligned with my major. Maybe assisting a professor with research instead of stacking books. That way I'm earning and learning at the same time. Otherwise, it just feels like trading precious study hours for tasks that don't contribute to my long-term goals.
Speaker 2

That's a fair point. I wouldn't say no to a more relevant job either. But still, even a simple job teaches discipline. And let's be real not all of us can get those research assistant roles. Sometimes starting with a basic job can actually open doors to those better opportunities later on.
Speaker 3

Well, if I'm going to work, I'd want it to mean something beyond the pay check. Otherwise, I'd rather focus on my grades. There has to be a balance. Burnout is real, and no amount of money is worth compromising both my health and academic performance.
facts: The discussion weighs campus part-time jobs against study demands and wellbeing.
Speaker 1 finds library work exhausting and insufficiently related to future career goals.
Speaker 1 would prefer flexible work-study or research assistance aligned with their major.
Speaker 2 says office work improves time management, financial independence, communication, reliability and discipline.
Speaker 2 accepts that relevant work is preferable but argues basic jobs can lead to better opportunities.
Speaker 3 describes café work causing stress, quitting after a month, and an unsustainable workload with 18 credits.
Speaker 3 prioritises health and grades and considers limited hours, while the group recognises the need for balance without fully agreeing on the value of campus work.
speaking-mock-5.sample: The students discuss whether campus part-time jobs are worthwhile. The first speaker says library work drains energy and offers little career relevance, preferring flexible work connected to their major, such as research assistance. The second values office work for income, better time management and transferable skills, arguing that basic jobs can also lead to better opportunities. The third describes quitting a café job because of stress and conflicting deadlines, and believes heavy study loads leave little room for employment. Although more relevant work appeals to the group, their views remain different. The discussion highlights balancing income and experience against academic performance and health.

speaking-mock-5.title: On-campus and off-campus housing
speaking-mock-5.narration: Three students are talking about their living experiences in on-campus dorms and off-campus housing.
turns: Speaker 1

I live in a house off campus with my friends. It's quite far from the school, but I am lucky because I live close to bus stops and it is very convenient. Also, our landlord is nice and takes care of things like cleaning and other problems around the house.
Speaker 2

I live in the school dormitory, which is very convenient, and there are places where I can study. Actually, I'd be quite happy to share a house with friends off campus, but the rent is too expensive. Also, I don't want to get up early, and the dormitory is very close to the teaching buildings.
Speaker 3

I also live in the school dormitory. If anything in the dorm breaks, it gets repaired soon, so students don't have to bother with it. Some friends living outside have problems with water and have to wait for a long time to have it fixed.
Speaker 1

That's honestly a huge advantage of living on campus. Even though our landlord is responsible and helpful, off-campus maintenance is really slow in general. We once had a water leakage issue and waited nearly a week for someone to fix it, which was really troublesome.
Speaker 2

While dorm life has plenty of benefits, it definitely comes with some annoying downsides as well. The fire alarm in our dormitory building often goes off in the middle of the night. Whenever the alarm goes off, we have to leave the building and wait until it has been checked. I'm fed up with being forced to get out of bed and evacuate outside because of fire alarms on cold winter nights.
Speaker 3

I totally agree with your opinion. I've experienced two fire alarms in the dorm, and both times they were caused by someone using a toaster illegally in the building. Can't they find the people who are cooking illegally and deal with them more quickly? Still, I think the system is quite safe, so I accept this accommodation plan.
Speaker 1

I had no idea dorm life had such annoying safety issues. Living off-campus definitely gives us more private space and flexible schedules. We can cook freely in our own kitchen without violating any campus rules, and we never suffer from sudden fire alarms at night.
Speaker 2

That sounds really relaxing, but off-campus accommodation still has obvious drawbacks. Apart from the high rent and slow maintenance, you also have to spend plenty of time on daily housework and commuting every single day.
Speaker 3

Exactly. Every living option has its own pros and cons. On-campus dorms are affordable, safe and time-saving, while off-campus houses provide more freedom and privacy. It all depends on personal study habits and lifestyle choices.
facts: The students compare on-campus dormitories with off-campus shared housing.
Speaker 1 values living with friends off campus, nearby buses, privacy, freedom and flexible cooking, but describes slow repairs.
Speaker 2 values dormitory convenience, study spaces, affordability and proximity to teaching buildings.
Speakers 2 and 3 complain about night-time fire alarms and evacuations; Speaker 3 still considers the dormitory safe.
Speaker 3 highlights quick on-campus repairs, unlike some off-campus water problems.
Speaker 2 notes that off-campus housing adds rent, maintenance, housework and commuting burdens.
Speaker 3 concludes that each option has trade-offs and the choice depends on study habits and lifestyle.

The first speaker enjoys sharing a house with friends, nearby transport and greater privacy and freedom, but acknowledges that repairs can be slow. The second values affordable dormitory accommodation close to classrooms and study spaces, while the third highlights prompt maintenance. However, both dormitory residents complain about disruptive fire alarms at night, although the third still considers the system safe. The second also notes the higher rent, housework and commuting associated with living off campus. They conclude that dormitories offer convenience and affordability, whereas private housing offers independence, and the best choice depends on individual habits and priorities.

speaking-mock-5.title: A workshop has moved
speaking-mock-5.text: You are helping run a university workshop. The original room has become unavailable, so the session has moved to a building five minutes away and will start fifteen minutes later. Several students are waiting outside the original room. What would you say to the waiting students?
speaking-mock-5.sample: Hi everyone, our workshop has moved because this room is unavailable. It will now be in another building about five minutes away and start fifteen minutes later. I can show you where to go. Thank you for your patience.
facts: Communicate the purpose of the situation directly to the intended person.
Offer a relevant request, explanation or practical response consistent with the situation.

speaking-mock-5.name: Respond to a Situation
speaking-mock-5.instruction: Read the situation. Speak directly to the person indicated and respond to the final question.
speaking-mock-5.title: Quiet time for an interview
speaking-mock-5.text: You have an important online interview tomorrow morning. Your housemate usually practises the guitar in the room next to yours at that time. You want to ask them to practise later that day so you can have a quiet interview. What would you say to your housemate?
speaking-mock-5.sample: Hi, I have an online interview tomorrow morning, which is when you usually practise guitar. Could you practise later that day so I have a quiet space for the call? I would appreciate it, and we can work out a time together.
facts: Communicate the purpose of the situation directly to the intended person.
Offer a relevant request, explanation or practical response consistent with the situation.
